en: In the northern direction there exists a king of mountains named Himālaya, whose essence is divine;
plunging into the eastern and western oceans, he stands like a measuring rod for the earth.
When Mera stood as the milker, skilled in the act of milking, and all the mountains conceived him as the calf,
they milked from the earth— as directed by Prithu— the radiant jewels and the great medicinal herbs.
For Him, from whom an endless stream of jewels originates, even the snow did not become a destroyer of his splendor;
for a single defect is submerged in a collection of virtues, like the spot on the moon amidst its rays.

And he who, with his peaks, bears a richness of minerals that produces the playful ornaments of the celestial nymphs, appearing like an untimely twilight with its colors distributed by scattered fragments of clouds.
Having sought shelter beneath the shadows of clouds moving as far as their mountain ridges,
the perfected ones (siddhas), distressed by the rains, take refuge upon its sun-drenched peaks.

In that place, even without seeing the tracks of the elephants they have slain, the Kirātas discern the path of the lions by means of pearls released from the hollows of their claws, which have been washed clean of blood by the flow of frost.
Where birch-bark, reddened by the spots of elephants and inscribed with letters using mineral pigments,
serves as the medium for love-letters written by the beautiful Vidyādhara maidens.
Filling the hollows of the *kīcaka* reeds with the wind rising from the mouths of its caves,
it seems as if it wishes to provide the musical tones for the *kiṃnaras* who are about to sing aloud.
There, the fragrance produced by the oozing sap of the *sarala* trees, which were rubbed against by elephants to relieve the itching of their temples,
perfumes the mountain ridges.
There, for the forest-dwellers accompanied by their wives, the medicinal herbs— whose luster clings to the interior of their cave-dwellings— serve as oil-less lamps for lovemaking during the night.

Even on a path where the snow has turned to solid ice, the horse-faced women do not break their slow gait, though they are distressed by the heavy weight of their hips and breasts, as they cause pain to their toes and heels.
He who protects the darkness hidden in caves from the sun, as if it were afraid of the day—
even when it has approached for refuge in a lowly state, the high-minded truly feel a sense of ownership toward it.
Where the female yaks, white as moonbeams, move here and there with the beauty of their tossing tails,
making the name "King of Mountains" meaningful for him through those yak-tail fans.
Where, for the Kimpuruṣa women who are embarrassed when their garments are snatched away,
the clouds— whose forms hang over the doorways of the mountain caves— spontaneously become their privacy screens.
The breeze there, which carries the spray from the cascades of the Bhāgīrathī, repeatedly shakes the deodar trees,
and which scatters the plumage of peacocks, is enjoyed by the Kirātas who are in pursuit of deer.
The sun, revolving below, awakens with its upward-pointing rays the lotuses that remain after being gathered by the hands of the Seven Sages, which grow in the lakes situated above him.
Observing that he was the source of the sacrificial components and that his essence was capable of supporting the earth,
Prajāpati himself established him in the lordship of the mountains, assigning him a share in the sacrifice.

Knowing the principles of stability and desiring the perpetuation of his lineage, that friend of Meru, who was worthy of honor even by sages, married according to the prescribed rites Menā— the daughter of the Pitṛs— who was a fit match for himself and possessed of a mind [attuned to his].
Then, as time passed and the occasion for sexual union appropriate to their nature arose,
a child was conceived by the wife of the king of mountains, who was bearing her delightful youth.
She gave birth to Maināka, who was destined to be enjoyed by the wives of the Nāgas and who formed a bond of friendship with the ocean;
he remained unaware of the wounds from the thunderbolt even when the enemy of Vṛtra, the cutter of wings, was enraged.
Then Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa and former wife of Bhava, being urged by her father’s contempt,
cast off her body through yoga and entered the daughter of the Mountain for the sake of rebirth.

By that lord of the mountains, she, Samādhimatī, gave birth to a worthy [son], just as prosperity arises through the quality of perseverance in a policy that is sound in application and unimpaired. Ks_1.22.
With the quarters of the sky serene, the winds free from dust, and a rain of flowers following immediately upon the sound of conchs,
that day of his birth became for the sake of the happiness of all embodied beings, both stationary and moving.
With that daughter, whose halo of radiance was shimmering, the mother shone all the more brightly,
like the earth of Mount Vidūra with a sprout of jewels bursting forth at the sound of a new cloud.
Day by day increasing and having attained her rise like a digit of the moon,
she nurtured special qualities consisting of loveliness, just as the intervening lunar phases nurture further variations of moonlight.

Her kinsmen called that beloved of her relatives by her family name, Pārvatī; but when she was forbidden from asceticism by her mother with the cry "O Um!", that fair-faced girl thereafter assumed the name Umā.
Although the king had other sons, his gaze never reached satiety upon that particular offspring;
for the swarm of bees has a special attachment to the mango blossom among the countless flowers of spring.
Like a lamp with its flame of great radiance, like the path to the triple heaven with its three-fold course,
or like a wise man with refined speech— he was both purified and adorned by her.
In her childhood, she took delight in the sand-pavilions of the Mandākinī, with balls and artificial dolls,
as she stood in the midst of her friends, as if repeatedly experiencing the essence of play.

At the time of instruction, the sciences acquired in previous births approached her— who possessed firm teaching— just as rows of swans approach the Ganges in autumn, or as natural radiances approach a great medicinal herb at night.
Then she attained that age which follows childhood— an unadorned ornament for her slender form, a non-liquor intoxicant that produces madness, and a weapon of Love distinct from flowers.
Her body, radiant with its four-square symmetry, was brought to full bloom by fresh youth, like a painting revealed by a brush or a lotus opened by the rays of the sun.
As his feet were set down upon the earth, the radiance from the nails of his elevated big toes seemed to pour forth passion;
thus his two feet brought to the ground the unstable splendor of land-lotuses.
As they moved with playful and graceful strides, that lady of supple limbs was followed by royal swans,
eager for instruction and wishing to acquire the tinkling of her anklets.
When the Creator fashioned her two beautiful shanks— round, tapering, and not too long—
it was as if he exerted all his effort toward the production of beauty for the sake of fashioning the rest of her limbs.
The trunks of the lord of serpents, because they are rough to the touch, and the various plantain trees, because they are exclusively cool—
though they may attain a voluminous form in the world, they have become excluded from being comparisons for her thighs.
Indeed, by this much alone, the region of the waist of the blameless lady— whose beauty was already inferable—
was made to shine by the placement of the girdle-string, which was later placed upon the lap that no other woman could ever desire.
Having entered the hollow of her deep navel,
the slender line of new hair shone like the dark radiance of the central gem of her girdle, having passed beyond its knot.
With her waist slender as the middle of a sacrificial altar, that young woman bore three beautiful folds of skin,
like a staircase constructed by fresh youth for the ascent of the God of Love.
The two pale breasts of the lotus-eyed woman grew so large, pressing against one another,
that not even a space as thin as a lotus fiber could be found between them, which were dark at their nipples.
It is my conjecture that her two arms possess a delicacy even greater than that of the śirīṣa flower,
for they were used as nooses around the necks of Śiva and the Fish-Bannered God (Kāma), even though the latter had been defeated.
Between her neck, which was made beautiful by her breasts, and her smooth string of pearls,
there arose a mutual relationship of ornament and the object to be adorned, as each produced beauty for the other.
Having gone to the moon, Lakṣmī does not enjoy the qualities of the lotus; and having taken refuge in the lotus, she does not possess the lunar splendor.
But having reached Umā’s face, the fickle goddess attained a joy that partakes of both.
If there were a flower set upon a fresh sprout, or a pearl resting upon bright coral,
it might then resemble her radiant smile as its luster spreads across her copper-hued lips.
When she, whose speech was noble, spoke with a voice that seemed to distill nectar, even the cuckoo—
though it be a bird nourished by others— became discordant to the listener, like a lute being struck out of tune.
The tremulous glance of the long-eyed woman, indistinguishable from a blue lotus in a strong breeze,
was taken up by her from the female deer, or rather, it was taken up by the female deer from her.

Beholding that beauty of her two curved eyebrows, which was as if fashioned from a rod of collyrium and was so skillful in its playfulness, the God of Love abandoned his pride in the loveliness of his own bow.
If animals possessed a sense of shame in their hearts, there is no doubt that upon beholding that mass of hair belonging to the daughter of the Mountain King,
the yak-cows would surely let go of their fondness for their own tails.
With a collection of all comparable substances arranged in their respective places,
she was fashioned by the Creator with great effort, as if out of a desire to behold beauty gathered in a single spot.
Once, it is said, Nārada, who wanders at will, beheld that maiden in the presence of her father and,
out of affection, prophesied that she would become the sole wife of Hara, sharing half of his body.
Therefore, although she had reached a marriageable age, the Guru remained with his desire for other brides stilled;
for no other fires, even when purified by mantras, are worthy of receiving the sacrificial oblation except the fire of Śiva himself.
For the Mountain was unable to make the God of Gods accept his daughter when she was not asked for;
a virtuous man, out of fear of rejecting a request, maintains neutrality even regarding a desired object.
From the very moment that beautiful-toothed lady cast off her body in her previous birth out of anger toward Dakṣa,
the Lord of Creatures became free from attachment and ceased to possess anything.

Clad in animal skins and with his senses restrained for the sake of austerity, he took up residence on a certain plateau of the Himalayas— sprinkled by the flow of the Gaṅgā, fragrant with musk, and where the *kiṃnaras* sang softly— amidst the deodar trees.
Adorned with clusters of *nameru* blossoms as their ear-ornaments, wearing soft birch-bark garments, and smeared with red arsenic, the Gaṇas sat upon rocky surfaces covered with bitumen.
Scratching with the tips of his hooves the rocks that were masses of frost, the humped bull,
lowing with pride, let out a roar— unbearable to the sound of a lion— that was somehow perceived by the terrified gavayas.

Having established the fire there, the Lord of Eight Forms— who himself is the ordainer of the fruits of asceticism— performed penance with some particular desire, having kindled the fire with fuel as his own other manifestation.
Having honored with a priceless offering that one who is himself honored by the inhabitants of heaven,
the Lord of Mountains commanded his daughter, who was purified and accompanied by her friends, to attend upon him.
Even though she was an adversary to his meditative concentration, Śiva permitted her to listen;
for those whose minds do not waver even when a cause for transformation is present—they alone are the steadfast.
Gathering flowers for offerings, skilled in sweeping the altar, and bringing water for her observances as well as sacrificial grass,
that fair-haired woman attended upon Giriśa every day, her fatigue dispelled by the rays of the moon upon his head.
At that time, the gods, oppressed by Tāraka,
went to the abode of Svayambhū, placing Turāsāha at their head.
To them, whose splendor of countenance had faded, Brahmā appeared,
like the radiant sun appearing in the morning to lotus ponds whose blossoms have closed.
Then they all, having prostrated themselves, waited upon the Lord of Speech, the sustainer of all, who faces every direction, with meaningful words.
Salutations to you, the threefold form, who existed as the solitary Self prior to creation,
and who subsequently underwent differentiation for the sake of the division of the three qualities.
O Unborn One, because the infallible seed sown by you within the waters has produced this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings, you are celebrated as its source.
Manifesting your majesty through three states,
you alone have become the cause of dissolution, maintenance, and creation.
Woman and man are two parts of your own self, whose form has been divided out of a desire to create;
they alone are remembered as the parents of the creation that partakes of procreation.
For you, whose day and night are divided according to your own measure of time,
sleep and waking are the dissolution and emergence of all beings.

You are the source of the world, yet you are without source; you are the end of the world, yet you are without end. You are the beginning of the world, yet you are without beginning; you are the lord of the world, yet you are without a lord.
You know yourself by yourself; you create yourself by yourself;
and through your own creative power, you dissolve back into yourself alone.
You are fluid, solid, and firm; gross, subtle, light, and heavy;
manifest and unmanifest; you possess sovereign will over all your manifestations.
Of those words whose opening is the *praṇava*, whose utterance follows three methods,
whose ritual action is sacrifice, and whose fruit is heaven— you are the source of them.
They declare you to be primordial nature (prakṛti), which sets in motion the goals of the person;
yet they know you alone to be the indifferent person (puruṣa) who perceives that nature.
You are the father even of the ancestors, the deity even of the gods;
you are higher than the highest, and the ordainer even of the ordainers.
You alone are the oblation and the priest, the food and the eternal eater;
you are the object of knowledge and the knower, the meditator and that which is to be meditated upon as the Supreme.
Having heard these truthful and heart-touching praises from them,
the Creator, inclined toward grace, replied to the inhabitants of heaven.
For that ancient poet, the fourfold activity of words as uttered from the mouth of the Four-faced One became fully realized.
Welcome to you, O mighty-armed ones of abundant prowess, who have arrived simultaneously, upholding your respective offices by means of your powers.
Why is it that your faces do not bear their own natural luster as they did before, appearing like stars whose light is obscured by frost? (Ks 2.19)
Due to the subsiding of its flames, this thunderbolt of the slayer of Vṛtra appears as if its edge has been blunted, with the celestial weapon no longer emitted from it.
Moreover, this noose of Varuṇa, once irresistible to his enemies,
has now fallen into a state of wretchedness, its power neutralized by a mantra, like that of a serpent.
With his mace cast aside, his arm is like a tree with broken branches, as if proclaiming the defeat that has become a thorn in Kubera’s mind.
Even Yama, scratching the ground with his staff whose luster has faded,
treats this [world] as lightly as a firebrand, even though it is not fruitless.
And how is it that these suns, cooled by the exhaustion of their heat,
have become so utterly beautiful to behold, as if they were figures depicted in a painting?
From the agitation of the winds, a break in their momentum is inferred,
just as the obstruction of a current of water is inferred from its movement upstream.
Even the heads of the Rudras, with the tips of their crescent moons hanging from their bound topknots,
proclaim their wounded *huṃkāra* cries.
Having first attained your established footing, have you now been turned back by others—just as general rules are set aside by more powerful exceptions? (2.27)
Therefore speak, my children: what do you seek by having come here?
For while the creation of the worlds rests with me, their protection is established in you.
Then Vāsava urged his preceptor with a thousand eyes, which shone like a bed of lotuses stirred by a gentle breeze.
With his two eyes, which surpassed the thousand eyes of Hari,
Vācaspati spoke thus with palms joined in reverence to the one seated upon the lotus.
Thus, O Blessed One, as you have said: "Our state has been seized by others;
how is it, O Lord, that you whose self is individually appointed [to each] do not know? (Kṣ 2.31)
The great asura named Tāraka, swollen with the boon obtained from you,
has arisen like a comet for the destruction of the worlds.
The sun spreads its heat over him only as much as is required for the blossoming of the lotuses in the long ponds.
The moon always attends upon him with all its digits;
it does not withhold even the single digit that serves as the crest-jewel for Hara.
In the garden, the wind, its movement checked by the fear of stealing the flowers,
does not blow at his side with a force greater than that of a palm-leaf fan.
Abandoning their seasonal succession, the seasons attend upon him like common gardeners, intent on providing an abundance of flowers.
The lord of rivers waits within his waters for those jewels suitable to be presented to him, until their emergence, by whatever means possible.
And at night, serpents headed by Vāsuki, with the crests of their jewels blazing, attend upon him like steady lamps.
Even Indra, seeking the favor bestowed by him, repeatedly gratifies him with ornaments from the wish-fulfilling tree brought by his messengers.
Even when propitiated in this manner, the wicked man continues to afflict the three worlds;
he is pacified by retaliation, not by kindness.
By him, the trees of the Nandana grove— whose sprouts were tenderly plucked by the hands of the immortal maidens— are made to bear the marks of cutting and falling.
For while he sleeps, he is fanned by the captive celestial women with chowries that release showers of tear-drops and carry the common air of his breath.
Having uprooted the peaks of Mount Meru, which had been trampled by the hooves of the gods' horses,
he fashioned pleasure-mountains within his own palaces.
Now, the ponds are the abode of the golden lotuses and crops, containing only the water of the Mandākinī, turbid with the ichor of the elephants of the quarters.
The joy of beholding the world is not experienced by the denizens of heaven,
for the paths to their celestial chariots have become impassable due to the fear of his descent.
While the sacrifices are being performed with oblations gathered by the sacrificers,
that master of illusions seizes from us the offerings before the very eyes of the Jātavedas.
And by him was carried away that jewel among horses, Uccaiḥśravas,
who was like Indra’s fame embodied after having been acquired over a long period of time.
Against that cruel one, all our stratagems were rendered ineffective,
like medicinal herbs against a complication of the three humors (sāṃnipātika) in a powerful disease.
Where our hope for victory was met by the flame arising from the impact of that discus of Hari, it was placed upon his neck like a golden ornament.
Today, his elephants— having conquered Airāvata— practice their charging against the slopes of clouds such as Puṣkara and Āvartaka.
Therefore, O All-pervading Lord, we desire that you create a commander for the sake of quelling him,
just as those seeking liberation seek the Dharma that severs the bonds of karma to end worldly existence.
Placing him at the forefront, the breaker of mountain peaks (Indra) will recover from his enemies the Goddess of Victory, like a captive woman, for he is the protector of the celestial armies.
When those words had ceased, the Self-born One uttered a speech that surpassed in excellence the rain that follows a thunderclap.
Your desire shall be fulfilled; let some time be awaited.
However, I will not personally undertake the labor of creation for its accomplishment.
That Daitya, having attained prosperity from this very source, ought not to meet his destruction from this same source;
for even a poison-tree, having been nurtured by oneself, is improper to cut down.
This very world was chosen by him previously, and I promised it to him as a boon;
for his ascetic power, which was sufficient to burn the worlds, has been neutralized by that boon.
Who could withstand him, that warrior ever-ready for battle, in combat—
save for one born from a portion of the seed of the blue-and-red-hued [Śiva]?
For that god is the supreme light established beyond darkness;
his power and majesty cannot be encompassed by me, nor by Viṣṇu.
O Umās, with your forms, strive to attract the mind of Śambhu— which is stilled by self-restraint— just as a magnet attracts iron.
Both are indeed capable of bearing the power bestowed by both;
whether it be that [form] of Śambhu or my own form consisting of water.
Having attained the command of your armies, that blue-throated one shall,
through the manifestations of his prowess, release the braided locks of the captive goddesses.
Having thus addressed the gods, Viśvayoni vanished;
and they too, having resolved upon their duties in their minds, returned to heaven.
Having resolved upon Kandarpa for that task, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) went there with a mind whose speed was doubled by the urgency of accomplishing his purpose.
Then the Flower-Bowed God, having slung upon his neck a bow whose beautiful tips were like the creeper-like brows of playful women and which was marked with the impressions of Rati’s bracelets,
approached the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices with joined palms, while his companion, the Spring, held in his hand the mango sprout that serves as his arrow.
Upon him, Indra’s thousand eyes fell simultaneously, abandoning the thirty gods;
for the respect shown by masters toward their dependents is generally fickle, depending as it does upon their perceived utility.
Having been granted the ground by Vāsava with the words, "Sit here close to my seat," she welcomed her lord’s favor with her head bowed and began to speak to him thus in private: Kumārasambhava 3.2.
Command me, O Knower of the distinctions of men, whatever is to be done by you in the worlds;
I desire that the favor arising from your remembrance be further increased by your command.
By whom, desiring a place among you, has this envy been produced through excessively long austerities—
[an envy] that lasts only as long as he remains obedient to the command of my bow, upon which an arrow is already fixed?
Who, being unconvinced, has entered the path of liberation out of fear of the afflictions of rebirth?
Let him remain bound for a long time by the sidelong glances of beautiful women, so skillful with their arched brows.

Tell me, for whose sake—though he has been taught statecraft even by Uśanas—shall I afflict your enemy’s wealth and virtue, while you employ passion as a spy? Like a swollen torrent against the banks of a river, I shall destroy him.

Why do you desire that woman of shapely hips— who was devoted to the vow of fidelity to one husband and whose character was marked by austerity— whose fickle mind had been captivated by your beauty, and who now casts aside her shame and throws her arms around your neck of her own accord?
O passionate one, by which angry woman were you rejected while prostrate at her feet for the offense of being unfaithful in love—
that woman whose body I shall now cause to feel such deep remorse that it will seek refuge only in a bed of young shoots?
Be gracious; O Hero, let the thunderbolt rest. Which enemy of the gods would fear my arrows, his prowess of arm rendered futile, even by women whose lips quiver with anger?

"By your grace, even though my only weapon is flowers, having obtained Spring alone as my companion, I could cause even Hara, the wielder of the Pināka bow, to lose his fortitude; what then of other mere archers?"

Then, having lowered his foot from the region of his thigh—a foot worthy of a footstool by virtue of its treading upon others—Indra spoke thus to Kāma, who had manifested his full power for the sake of his intended purpose: Kāmandakīya-nītisāra 3.11.
"Friend, all this is fitting in you; both my weapons, the thunderbolt and yourself, are present.
The thunderbolt is blunted against those great in ascetic power and heroism, but you are all-pervading and effective."
I recognize your strength; therefore, I shall indeed appoint you, who are equal to myself, to this weighty task.
Śeṣa is assigned by Kṛṣṇa to bear his body, having regard for his quality as a mountain.
O Bull-bannered One, as you desire the path of the arrow, our task is now almost accomplished;
understand this: for those who enjoy the portions of the sacrifice, this alone is now their highest desire regarding their enemies.
For these gods desire a commander-in-chief born of valor for the sake of conquering existence;
and he, born from the body of Brahmā with his soul absorbed in Brahman, can be accomplished only by the falling of your arrow.

Therefore, strive to win the favor of Himavat’s daughter for that self-restrained one; for it was taught by the Self-born Creator that among women, she alone is capable of being the soil for the sowing of his seed.

"And by the command of my preceptor, that group of Apsarases— of whom I am a member— has been heard from the mouths of others that the daughter of the Mountain King attended upon Sthāṇu as he performed austerities on the mountain plateau."
Therefore, go for the sake of success and perform the work of the gods; this purpose must indeed be accomplished through another means.
It awaits you as its supreme condition, just as a sprout from a seed awaits water before its emergence.
In this matter of the gods' means for victory, the mastery of weapons depends on you alone;
for even an unestablished deed, if it is unique to a man, leads to his glory.
"O gods, these are your petitioners; the task belongs to all three worlds.
Your deed with the bow shall not be excessively violent—oh, how enviable is your prowess!"
O Manmatha, by virtue of your constant association with Madhu, even though not explicitly mentioned, wine is indeed your companion;
for who must give instructions to the wind, "Become the fanner of the fire"?
Saying "So be it," Madana set out, receiving his master's command upon his head as if it were a final decree;
then Indra touched his body with a hand made callous by the striking of Airāvata.
Followed with apprehension by his beloved friend Mādhava and by Rati,
he went to the Himalayan hermitage of Sthāṇu, having sought the accomplishment of his purpose through the sacrifice of his own body.
In that forest, Madhu, acting as an adversary to the penance and meditative concentration of the self-restrained sages,
expanded himself by assuming a form born of his own will, manifesting his egoistic power.
When the hot-rayed sun set out for the direction guarded by Kubera, transgressing the proper season,
the southern quarter released the wind from her mouth like a sigh born of resentment.
The aśoka tree immediately produced flowers along with new shoots from its very trunk;
it no longer required the touch of the feet of beautiful women adorned with jingling anklets.
When the fresh mango shoot, beautiful with its newly sprouted leaves, had reached completion,
Spring settled bees upon it as if they were the syllables of the name of the Mind-born God.
When its color was at its peak, the *karṇikāra* flower pained the mind with its lack of fragrance;
generally, the Creator’s activity is averse to the complete assembly of all qualities.
The extremely red palāśa flowers, curved like the young crescent moon because they had not yet blossomed,
shone like nail-marks upon the forest grounds that had just been joined by Spring.
Having displayed upon her face a tilaka, variegated with the application of collyrium and bees clinging to it,
the beauty of spring adorned her lip— resembling a mango sprout— with a passion as tender as the dawn.
Deer, their vision obstructed by particles of pollen from the blossoms of the *priyāla* trees,
wandered through the forest glades against the wind— intoxicated with rut and shedding rustling leaves.
The sweet warbling of the male cuckoo, whose throat was parched from tasting the mango sprouts,
became the very speech of the God of Love, skilled at shattering the pride of high-minded women.
With the departure of the snow, as the lips of the kimpuruṣa women became clear and the complexion of their faces turned pale,
the emergence of perspiration left its mark upon their decorative leaf-patterns.
Seeing that untimely onset of spring, the ascetics dwelling in the forest of Sthāṇu—
whose transformations were somehow restrained through effort— became masters of their minds with great difficulty.
When Madana, with his bow strung with flowers, had entered that place accompanied by Rati,
the pairs [of lovers] revealed their inner state through action, permeated by a surge of passion that had reached its ultimate height.
The bee, following its beloved, drank honey from the single vessel of a flower;
and the black antelope scratched with his horn the doe, whose eyes were closed at the touch.
The female elephant gave to the male elephant mouthfuls of water fragrant with lotus pollen from her own juices;
meanwhile, the Cakravāka bird honored his mate with half-eaten lotus stalks.

Between songs, the kimpuruṣa kissed the face of his beloved, which was beautiful with eyes rolling from the intoxication of flower-liquor, and upon which the lines of the leaf-design were slightly revived by droplets of perspiration.
Even the trees received the embrace of the vine-brides with their branch-arms bent low, as they bore breasts of full flower-clusters and were made charming by lips of shimmering young shoots.
Even though he had heard the song of the Apsarases at that moment, Hara became intent on meditative discernment;
for indeed, obstacles can never arise to shatter the concentration of those who are masters of themselves.
Then Nandin, standing at the door of the bower with a golden staff resting on his left forearm,
dismissed the attendants with a gesture of a single finger placed upon his mouth, saying, "Do not be fickle!"
By his command, the entire forest stood as if its activities were depicted in a painting: the trees were motionless, the bees were still, the birds were mute, and the movement of the deer had ceased.
Having avoided the precipice of false views, his desire, like the vanguard dust in a march,
entered the abode of meditation belonging to the Lord of Beings, where the branches of the *nameru* trees were entwined at its borders.
He beheld the three-eyed Lord, self-restrained, seated upon a dais of deodar wood covered with a tiger skin, his own physical fall now imminent.
With his upper body made steady by the paryaṅka posture, his shoulders evenly drawn back and straightened,
he sat like a blossoming lotus in the center of his lap due to the placement of his two palms turned upward.
He wears a mass of matted hair bound by a serpent, with a double-stranded rosary hanging from his ear,
and he bears a knotted black antelope skin that is especially darkened by contact with the luster of his throat.
With eyes whose pupils were somewhat bright, steady, and intense, which had ceased from the movement of the eyebrows,
and whose lashes did not blink, he fixed his gaze upon the tip of his nose with downward-turned rays of light.
Like a rain-cloud free from the fury of a storm, like a reservoir of waters without waves,
and like a lamp unmoved by the absence of wind due to the cessation of the internal airs, [he sat].
With sprouts of light emerging from his head, having found their path through the openings between his skull and eyes,
he eclipsed the beauty of the moon— a beauty more delicate than a lotus fiber— belonging to that infant.
Having established the mind— its functions restrained from the nine gates— within the heart and brought under control through meditative concentration,
one beholds that Self within oneself, which those who know the field recognize as the Imperishable.
Beholding from nearby the three-eyed Lord who was thus transformed, and who was unassailable even by the mind, Smara—
his hand failing through trepidation— could no longer perceive his bow or the arrow that had slipped from his own grasp.
Then the daughter of the King of Mountains appeared, escorted by two forest deities; her physical excellence seemed to kindle his vigor, which was already largely focused upon Nirvana.

She wore ornaments of spring flowers: *padmarāga* gems surpassed by *aśoka* blossoms, *karṇikāra* flowers drawn away from their golden luster, and *sinduvāra* flowers fashioned into clusters of pearls.
As if slightly bent by her breasts, wearing a garment with the hue of the rising sun,
she was like a moving, leafy creeper bending under the weight of fully formed clusters of blossoms.
The girdle of saffron filaments, slipping from her hips and hanging down again and again,
was like a second bowstring deposited there by Smara, who knows the proper place for it.
With her eyes flickering in agitation at every moment, she warded off with her play-lotus a bee that hovered near her bimba-red lip, its thirst increased by her fragrant breath.
Beholding her, whose every limb was faultless and who even caused shame to Rati herself,
the flower-bowed god once again hoped for the success of his purpose before the wielder of the trident, whose senses were conquered.
And Umā reached the entrance hall of Śambhu, who was about to become her husband;
and he, having beheld through yoga the supreme light known as the Inner Self, desisted from his practice.
Then, with the tips of the hoods of the lord of serpents somehow supporting the portion of the earth below him, the Lord,
gradually relinquishing his vital breath, broke his firm cross-legged posture.
Having prostrated before him, Nandin reported that the daughter of the mountain had arrived with a desire to serve;
and he ushered her in, for her entrance was permitted by a mere movement of her husband’s eyebrows.

After first prostrating herself, her two friends scattered at the feet of the Three-Eyed God a heap of flowers from the end of winter, gathered with their own hands and interspersed with bits of tender shoots.
Umā too, loosening a fresh *karṇikāra* flower that graced the midst of her dark tresses,
made a salutation with her head— its ear-pendant falling— to the one whose banner is the bull.
"Obtain a husband who will share no other wife"—this was spoken by Bhava as nothing but the truth;
for the utterances of the Lord never in this world result in a contrary meaning.
But Kāma, awaiting his opportunity to discharge his arrows, like a moth seeking to enter the mouth of a flame,
repeatedly touched the bowstring in the presence of Umā, having fixed his aim upon Hara.
Then Gaurī offered to Giriśa, the ascetic, with her copper-hued hand,
a rosary of lotus seeds from the Mandākinī that had been dried by the rays of the sun.
Out of affection for his supplicant, the Three-eyed Lord proceeded to accept her;
meanwhile, the Flower-bowed God fixed upon his bow an unerring arrow named Sammohana.
But Hara, his fortitude somewhat diminished like the ocean at the onset of moonrise,
fixed his eyes upon Umā’s face, where her lower lip was like the bimba fruit.
Even the daughter of the mountain, revealing her emotion through limbs resembling blossoming young kadamba flowers,
stood with her face beautifully turned aside and her eyes cast down.
Then the Three-Eyed One, having restrained his agitation of the senses through his mastery and power,
cast his gaze toward the ends of the quarters, desiring to see the cause of the transformation in his own mind.
He saw the Self-born One, with his fist placed at the corner of his right eye, his shoulder bent and his left foot drawn back,
having made his beautiful bow into a circle, ready to strike.
As his anger increased through his reflection upon asceticism, and his face became difficult to behold due to the knitting of his brows,
a fire with flickering flames suddenly burst forth, it is said, from his third eye.
Even as the words of the gods, "O Lord, withdraw your wrath! Withdraw it!
were still traveling through the sky, that fire born from the eye of Bhava reduced Madana to nothing but ashes.
With the onset of a delusion born of intense affliction that paralyzed the functions of her senses,
Rati— for a moment— seemed as if she had been granted a favor, since she remained unaware of her husband’s calamity.
Having swiftly shattered that obstacle to his asceticism like a thunderbolt splitting a lord of the forest,
the Lord of Beings, accompanied by his attendants and desiring to avoid contact with women, vanished from sight.

The daughter of the Mountain, too, having realized that her father’s desire for high status was in vain and considering her own graceful form, felt an even greater sense of shame in the presence of her two friends; thus, with a vacant mind, she somehow made her way toward her palace.
Immediately, the Mountain, taking his pitiable daughter— who had her eyes closed in fear of Rudra’s fury— upon his two arms,
moved along the path back like a celestial elephant carrying a lotus plant clinging to its tusks, his limbs stretched out by his speed.
Then the wife of Kāma, devoted to delusion and helpless, was awakened by Fate,
which was about to impose upon her the unbearable pain of fresh widowhood.
Intent on concentration, she opened her eyes wide as if at the end of a cosmic dissolution;
yet, even as they remained unsatiated, she did not perceive her beloved, who had been utterly vanished from sight.
Having cried out, "O lord of my life, are you alive? as she rose up, she saw before her on the ground nothing but the ashes from the fire of Śiva’s wrath in human form.
Then, once again overwhelmed, her breasts grey from embracing the earth,
she lamented with her hair disheveled, as if making the very ground share in her sorrow.
That which was the standard of comparison for the ornaments of amorous men because of its loveliness has now come to such a state; yet I do not break asunder—women are indeed hard-hearted.

Where indeed have you fled, having cast me away— my life depending entirely upon you— your friendship shattered in an instant, like a mass of water that has broken its dam and dispersed after scattering a lotus pond?
"You have done nothing displeasing to me, nor have I acted contrary to you;
why then is my sight not granted to Rati, who laments thus without cause?"
Do you remember, O Smara, the binding with the cords of my girdle whenever there was a slip of the tongue regarding my lineage,
or the blows from the blue lotuses used as ear-ornaments when my eyes were irritated by falling filaments?
I understand that what you said—"You dwell in my heart"—is a deception intended to please me;
for if this were not a mere conventional expression, how could Rati remain unharmed while you are bodiless?
I shall follow your path as one departing for a new journey to the next world;
this person has been deceived by fate, for indeed, the happiness of embodied beings depends entirely upon you.
O beloved, when the city streets are shrouded in the darkness of night, who else but you is capable of leading the wives of lovers— who are distressed by the sound of heavy rain— to their dwellings?
With eyes rolling red and stumbling at every step in their speech,
the intoxication of wine now serves only as a mockery for women when you are no longer present.
O Anaṅga, having realized that the body of your dear kinsman has been turned into mere words, the moon, its rising rendered fruitless,
will painfully waste away even as the dark fortnight passes.
Tell me now, to whom will this fresh mango blossom become an arrow— possessing a lovely stalk of greenish-red hue and heralded by the melodious song of the male cuckoo?
This row of bees has been employed by you many times for the purpose of stringing your bow;
now, with its piteous humming, it seems to lament for me as I am consumed by heavy grief.
Having again assumed his enchanting form, he rose up and once more commanded the cuckoo,
who is naturally skilled in sweet warbling, to serve as the messenger of Rati.
Having prostrated with my head, having entreated you, and having embraced you while trembling—
remembering those secret acts of lovemaking, I find no peace.
O expert in love, this seasonal adornment of flowers has been fashioned by you yourself upon my limbs; yet that beautiful body of yours is not seen.
"Come, make this left foot of mine— upon which you were remembered by the fierce gods even before the ritual preparation was complete— the very embodiment of passion."
O beloved, having come by the path of the moth, I shall once again take refuge in your lap,
before you are enticed away from heaven by the clever celestial nymphs.
"Separated from Madana, Rati has indeed lived for even a mere moment"—this reproach is established against me, O Beloved, even though I am following after you. Ks_4.21.
"How can I perform the final adornment for you who have departed for the next world?
For both your body and your life have gone together to that unforeseen state."
I remember you straightening your arrow as it rested upon your lap while your bow lay across your thigh,
as you engaged in smiling conversation with Madhu and cast glances from the corners of your eyes.
Where indeed is your heart-pleasing friend Madhu, who has fitted his bow with flowers?
Surely he too has not been sent by the fierce-tempered wielder of the Pināka to the same destination as his friend?
Then, pained in his heart as if by poisoned arrows by those words of lamentation,
Madhu revealed himself before her, distressed as she was, in order to offer her consolation.
Beholding him, she wept bitterly and beat her breast, which was pressed by her breasts;
for the sorrow of one's own kin arises before one as if with its doors wide open.
And thus she spoke to him in her distress: "Look, O friend, what remains of spring?
This ash, mottled like a dove, which is being scattered in fragments by the winds."
O Smara, grant him an audience now; this Mādhava is longing for you.
Indeed, while men's affection for beloved women may be unstable, it is certainly not fickle toward a friend.
Indeed, by this attendant standing at your side, the entire world, including the gods and the asuras,
has been made to obey your command with a bow whose string is a lotus fiber and whose arrows are delicate flowers.
Once gone, that friend of yours does not return, like a lamp extinguished by the wind;
behold me, his wick, scorched by the unbearable calamity that has befallen him.

Surely fate, by sparing me when it slew my beloved, has committed a half-destruction; for even though I am blameless, I am like a creeper on a tree that supports me, now broken by an elephant, destined to fall.
Therefore, let this duty toward your kinsmen be performed by you immediately:
surely convey me, who am distressed, from the fire to the presence of my husband.
The moonlight departs with the moon, and the lightning vanishes with the cloud;
for it is understood even by the insentient that women follow the path of their husbands.
With this very same fortunate ash from the body of my beloved, which has stained my breasts,
I shall fashion my form upon the fire as if upon a bed of fresh sprouts.
O gentle one, you have many times before assisted us in preparing a bed of flowers;
now, therefore, at my request made with prostrations and joined palms, quickly prepare my funeral pyre.
Thereafter, hasten the fire offered by me with the fanning of southern breezes;
for it is well known to you how Smara cannot endure even a moment without me.
"Furthermore, having made this arrangement, let a single handful of water be offered for both of us;
for in the next world, that kinsman of yours will drink it together with me, without dividing it."
And in the rite for the next world, O Mādhava, you should offer mango blossoms with their swaying shoots, dedicating them to Smara;
for the dear mango blossom is indeed your friend.
Thus Sarasvatī, born of the ether, took pity upon Rati who stood resolved on liberation from the gods,
just as the first rain takes pity on a small fish distressed by the drying up of its pond.
"O wife of the one whose weapon is flowers, your husband will not remain difficult to attain for long.
Listen to the deed by which he became like a moth in the flame of Hara’s eye."
The Lord of Creatures, his senses aroused, conceived a lustful desire for his own daughter;
then, having restrained that transformation, he was cursed by her and experienced this fruit.
When Hara, won over by her ascetic penance, shall marry Pārvatī, then he,
having attained his own happiness, will restore Smara to his own body.
Thus he spoke, when entreated for the sake of dharma, that Sarasvatī who sets the limit for the curse of Smara;
for both thunderbolts and nectar have the clouds as their source, and the clouds are masters over both.
Therefore, O beautiful one, protect this body which is destined for union with its beloved;
for at the end of the heat, a river whose waters were drunk by the sun is joined again by a flood.
In this way, a certain invisible being dispelled Rati’s resolve to die;
and because of that assurance, her kinsman, the flower-armed god, comforted her with words whose meaning was realized through his own conduct.
Then Madana’s wife, emaciated by her calamity, waited for the end of the upheaval,
like the crescent of the daytime moon, grey with the waning of its rays, waiting for the onset of night.

Thus, her hopes shattered by the wielder of the Pināka bow as he consumed the god of love before her very eyes, Pārvatī reproached her own beauty in her heart; for the fruit of loveliness is indeed good fortune among those one loves.
Resorting to meditative concentration through her own ascetic penances, she desired to make her beauty fruitful;
for otherwise, how could both such love and such a husband be obtained?
Having heard that her daughter had set out for asceticism, her mind fixed upon the Lord of the Mountains,
Menā embraced her with her chest and spoke, seeking to restrain her from the great vow of the sages.
The deities desired are present even in the home; where, my child, is asceticism, and where is your delicate form?
A *śirīṣa* flower might endure the tread of a bee, but not that of a bird.
Thus, though she instructed her daughter whose will was fixed, Menā was unable to restrain her from her exertion;
for who can turn back a mind that is firmly resolved upon its desired object, or water flowing toward a lower level?
Once, through the mouth of her close friend, that high-minded woman requested from her father— who understood her heart's desire—
permission for her own residence in the forest for the sake of ascetic discipline and meditative concentration, which culminate in the attainment of spiritual fruit.
Then, having been granted permission by her most venerable preceptor— who was satisfied with his own appropriate attachment—
Gaurī went to the peacock-crested peak of the mountain, which later became renowned among living beings by that very name.

Having cast off her necklace, she whose resolve was unshakable removed the sandalwood paste from her swaying body and bound on a bark garment tawny as the rising sun, its texture frayed by the fullness of her breasts.
Just as his face was renowned for being sweet with beautiful hair, so too it became sweet even with matted locks;
for a lotus does not shine only when accompanied by swarms of bees, but also when joined with clinging moss.
Every moment, she wore for her vow a triple-stranded girdle of muñja grass that caused her hair to stand on end;
by its presence, the place where her waistband had previously been fastened became flushed with passion.
Her hand, which had been accustomed to lower lips from which passion had departed and to a ball reddened by the cosmetic paste of her breasts,
now became devoted to a rosary of beads, its fingers scarred by the plucking of blades of *kuśa* grass.
She who used to feel distressed even by the flowers from her own hair fallen while turning upon a costly bed,
now lay down using only her creeper-like arms as a pillow, sitting instead upon the bare ground alone.
Furthermore, as she remained under a vow, she deposited both of these things as if in a trust with two others:
her graceful gestures upon slender creepers, and her tremulous glances among the female deer.
Unwearied, she herself nurtured the saplings with water flowing from her jar-breasts— those trees for whom Guha would never cease his parental affection, as if they were his own first-born sons.
And the deer, cherished by her through the offering of handfuls of wild seeds, placed such trust in her that she,
out of curiosity, would measure her own eyes against theirs in the presence of her friends.

Sages who desired to see her approached her as she had performed her ablutions, offered oblations into the sacred fire, was clad in an upper garment of bark, and was engaged in study; for among those advanced in dharma, age is not taken into account.
That penance grove became purifying: it had long since abandoned its former hostility and envy; its trees honored guests with their desired fruits; and fires were maintained within its new leaf-huts.
When she perceived that the desired fruit could not be obtained by her previous austerities and meditative concentration alone,
she then disregarded the delicacy of her own body and began to perform great penance.
She, who grew weary even by the play of a ball, plunged into the conduct of the sages;
for her body was surely fashioned from golden lotuses, being both soft by nature and yet possessed of firm strength.
Standing in the midst of four blazing sacrificial fires on a pure spot, the slender-waisted woman of radiant smiles,
having surpassed with her own brilliance the light that dazzles the eyes, gazed at the sun with an undivided gaze.
Thus scorched by the rays of the sun, his face assumed the beauty of a lotus;
only in the corners of his long eyes did a trace of darkness gradually settle.
Water presented unasked and the rays of the moon, which consists solely of nectar, were indeed her means for the rite of breaking her fast;
she possessed no implements other than the way of life of a tree.
Intensely heated by various fires— both those moving through the sky and those fueled by wood—
at the end of the summer heat, when drenched by fresh rains, the earth released its upward-moving warmth along with her.

The first drops of rain paused for a moment upon her eyelashes, struck her lower lip, were ground to powder by falling upon the fullness of her breasts, and having slipped across her folds, reached her navel only after a long time.
He gazed upon her, who lay upon a stone slab and dwelt without a shelter amidst incessant internal winds and rains,
as if the nights stood there as witnesses to his great asceticism with eyes opened by flashes of lightning.
Devoted to dwelling in the water, she spent the nights of the month of Sahasya amidst winds scattering intense frost;
compassionate, she watched the pair of ruddy geese separated before her, crying out to one another.
At night, with her lotus-scented mouth, its lower lip shining as it trembled,
she seemed to restore the abundance of lotuses to the waters, which had been destroyed by a shower of frost.
Subsisting on the leaves of trees that have fallen of their own accord is indeed the highest limit of asceticism;
yet she has even abandoned that, and therefore those who know the past call that sweet-spoken lady "Aparṇā" (the Leafless One).
Day and night, with such vows as these, she withered her own body, which was as delicate as a lotus stalk;
by means of her ascetic bodies, she cast far below the ascetics who had acquired their merit through harsh penances.
Then, wearing a deerskin and a bark garment, bold in speech and as if blazing with the splendor consisting of the Veda,
a certain matted-haired ascetic entered the penance grove like the first stage of life incarnate.
Pārvatī went out to meet him with a hospitable reception preceded by great respect;
for even among those whose minds are fixed on equanimity, there are actions of profound reverence toward those distinguished by their physical form.
Having accepted the hospitality offered according to the prescribed rites and having dispelled his fatigue for a moment,
he looked at Umā with a straightforward gaze and proceeded to speak, without abandoning the proper sequence of discourse.

Is the sacrificial wood and *kuśa* grass easily available for your rites? Are there waters sufficient for the performance of your ablutions? Do you apply yourself to austerity according to your capacity? For the body is indeed the primary instrument for the practice of dharma.
Moreover, the sprouts of these creepers, nourished by the water poured forth by you,
possess a continuous quality such that they rival the redness of your teeth, which has long since abandoned its application of lac-dye.
O lotus-eyed one, is your mind also inclined toward the deer that steal the affection for the darbha grass held in your hand—
those which, with their flickering eyes, seem to emulate the beauty of yours?
O Pārvatī, that saying which claims that beauty does not lead to sinful conduct is unfailing; for indeed, O lady of noble vision, your character has become a source of instruction even for ascetics.

This mountain, along with its lineage, has been purified not so much by the waters of the Ganges falling from heaven— which mock the offerings scattered by the Seven Sages— as by your own stainless deeds.

"O noble lady, because you have accepted and practiced this Dharma alone— having turned your mind away from the objects of wealth and desire— it appears to me today that Dharma is the most distinguished essence of the three aims of life."

O lady of graceful limbs, you should not consider me as someone superior to yourself, especially since you have already shown me such exceptional honor; for it is said that among the virtuous, friendship with the wise is formed by walking seven steps together.
Therefore, O lady rich in asceticism, this person, whose fickleness is natural to his status as a twice-born, desires to ask you something; if it is not a secret, you should deign to answer.

Birth in a noble family, a body arisen like the very beauty of the three worlds belonging to the First Creator, sovereignty and happiness beyond seeking, and fresh youth—tell me, what fruit of asceticism could there be greater than this? Ks_5.41.
"Indeed, such a resolve may arise even from unbearable adversity for high-minded women;
yet, O slender-waisted one, that [resolve] is not seen in you when your mind is directed toward the path of reflection."
This form of yours is incapable of being overcome by grief; O fair-browed one, whence could there be such humiliation in your father’s house?
There is no assault from another upon you—who would stretch out a hand toward the needle-like jewel of a serpent?
Why did you cast aside your ornaments in your youth and don this bark garment that graces old age? Tell me, if the night—bright with the moon and stars—is not better suited for the dawn?
If you seek heaven, your labor is in vain; for the regions of your father are the very lands of the gods.
Or, if you seek a husband, enough with this asceticism; for one does not search for a jewel when it is already being sought after.
What has been announced by your hot sighs causes my mind to sink into doubt:
since he who is to be sought by you is not seen, how could he be one whose favor is difficult to obtain even when sought?

Oh! What a steadfast youth must be your beloved, who, since your ear-lotuses have long since perished, has neglected these matted locks, tawny at their tips like ripened rice, hanging loosely upon your cheeks.
Whose heart would not grieve upon seeing you, emaciated by the vows of a sage, your ornaments scorched by the sun, like the crescent of the moon seen by day?

I know that your beloved has been deceived by the intoxication of his own good fortune; for, though you cast fourfold glances, he does not long make his own face the target of those eyes with their curved lashes.
"How long will you weary yourself, O Gaurī? I too possess ascetic merit accumulated in my former stage of life;
receive with half of that the boon you desire, and I wish to know it well."
Having entered thus, she was addressed by the twice-born man, yet she was unable to declare what was in her mind;
then she cast her gaze, with eyes whose collyrium had been washed away, toward her friend standing at her side.
Her friend said to that religious student: "Listen, O virtuous one, if you have curiosity as to why she has made her body—a means for asceticism—like a lotus for warding off the heat."
This proud woman, having held in contempt the lords of the four quarters, beginning with Mahendra,
desires to obtain as her husband the wielder of the Pināka bow, who cannot be won by physical beauty because of his subjugation of Madana.
In former times, an arrow turned back by an unbearable roar failed to reach the face of the Enemy of Tripura;
yet that very same shaft struck this woman in the heart with a wide-reaching impact, even though the flower-bowed god’s body was already shattered.
From that time forth, maddened in her father’s house, with her curls greyed by sandalwood paste used as a forehead mark,
the young girl never found any peace, even upon stone slabs as cold as masses of snow.

As the Pināka-wielder performed his dance of sublime beauty, this daughter of the Kinnara king caused her companions in the forest concert to weep, with words faltering from a throat choked with tears.

When three-quarters of the night remained, she suddenly opened her eyes for a moment and, with arms thrown around his neck though he was not there, cried out in an inaudible voice, "O Blue-throated One, where are you going? (Ks 5.57)
"When you are called 'all-pervading' by the wise, how is it that you do not know this person situated within your own being?
Thus was the moon-crested Lord reproached in secret by the innocent girl, who had drawn him with her own hand.
And when, searching for no other means to attain the state of the Lord of the World, she saw no other way,
then, with our permission and by the command of her teacher, she departed for the penance grove to practice austerities.
Even among these trees, which have themselves taken birth as her companions and serve as witnesses to her asceticism,
the fulfillment of her desire— centered upon the Moon-crested Lord— is not seen to be even approaching fruition.

I do not know when he—so difficult to obtain even when sought—will take this friend of mine under his protection; she who is emaciated by asceticism, gazed upon by her friends with eyes full of tears, and wasted by the drought of his absence, like the earth parched by a lack of rain.

Having been informed by her, who understood his gestures, that his true state was not concealed, the eternally handsome youth asked Umā, "O friend, is this indeed so? while concealing any outward sign of joy, as if it were a mere jest.
Then, offering a crystal rosary with her fingers folded into a bud-like shape in her upraised hand,
the Daughter of the Mountain spoke with measured words, having finally composed her speech after a long hesitation.
O best among those who know the Vedas, as you have heard, this person is eager to leap to a high station;
it is said that this asceticism is the means for attaining it, for there is no limit to the reach of one's desires.
Then the student said: "Maheśvara is well known to me; you, however, continue to seek him.
Considering that he delights in the practice of inauspicious things, I do not venture to follow your lead."
O you who are intent on an impossible object, how indeed will this hand of yours, with its marriage-thread still fastened,
endure being grasped for the first time by the hand of Śambhu, which encircles a serpent as a bracelet?
You yourself should first consider whether these two are ever worthy of union:
the bride’s silk garment marked with the sign of the swan, and the elephant hide raining down drops of blood.

Who indeed, even an enemy, would approve of your feet— marked with red lac— leaving their footprints upon the grounds of the dead strewn with disheveled hair, when they are already covered by a scattering of four-fold flower offerings?
Tell me, what could be more improper than this, which is easily available even to you:
that the dust of funeral ashes shall leave its mark upon these two breasts, the very seat of yellow sandalwood?

And this other mockery awaits you before you: when the great multitude beholds you—who were once carried by a king of elephants—mounted upon an old ox, they will have their faces turned toward smiles.
Now both have fallen into a state of lamentability through their longing for union with the Skull-bearer:
that radiant digit of the Moon, and you, who are the moonlight for the eyes of this world.
O fawn-eyed one, his body is three-eyed, his birth is unknown, and his wealth is revealed by his nakedness;
is there anything sought among suitors that exists even in part within this Three-Eyed One?
Turn your mind away from this unworthy desire; where are you, such as you are, and where is one endowed with auspicious marks?
The virtuous do not expect a Vedic consecration for the sacrificial post of a funeral stake.
Thus, as the twice-born spoke in opposition, she, her anger revealed by her trembling lower lip,
cast her eyes askance— reddened at the corners— with their creeper-like brows knit together.
And he said to him: "Surely you do not know Hara in his true essence, since you speak to me thus;
for the dull-witted hate the conduct of the Great-souled ones, which is unlike anything in the world and whose causes are inconceivable. (Ks 5.75)
Auspicious rites are practiced by one intent on averting misfortune or by one eager for prosperity;
but for the virtuous one who is the refuge of the world and free from desires, what need is there for these things that corrupt the mind with longing?
Though possessing nothing, he is the source of all prosperity; though his abode is the cremation ground, he is the Lord of the Three Worlds;
though he has a terrifying form, he is proclaimed as Śiva—there are none who truly know the Pināka-wielder as he really is.
Whether resplendent with ornaments or encircled by serpents, whether wearing an elephant hide or clad in fine silk,
whether bearing a skull-cup or having the moon as his crest— no single form can be discerned of the body of the Universal Form.
Having come into contact with his limbs, the dust of the funeral pyre's ashes certainly serves for purification;
for it is thus that the dust falling from the performance of dance and dramatic gestures is smeared upon the crests of the dwellers of heaven.
As he proceeds on his bull, Indra— whose vehicle consists of world-elephants with temporal juice flowing—
approaches him on foot and, bowing with his crown, reddens the toes of the bull’s feet with the pollen of blossoming *mandāra* flowers.
O Lord, although you intended to point out a fault, you have spoken rightly regarding the One Supreme:
"How could He, whom even the Self-born [Brahmā] acknowledges as his own cause, have His origin from a visible source? (Ks 5.81)
Enough with this dispute; let him remain exactly as you have heard him to be, in every respect.
My mind is fixed here, its sole essence being devotion; for one whose conduct is driven by desire does not heed what is censurable.
"Friend, let this boy be stopped; he wishes to speak further, as his upper lip is quivering.
Not only is he guilty who speaks ill of the great, but he who listens to such speech also shares in the sin. (Ks 5.83)
Saying, "Shall I go from here? the young woman, her bark garment strained by her breasts, began to move away;
but he whose banner bears the king of bulls, assuming his own form and smiling, took hold of her.

Beholding him, the daughter of the mountain king— her slender body trembling, her delicate limbs quivering, and lifting her raised foot to set it down— neither went forward nor remained still, like a river obstructed by a mountain on its path.

When the moon-crested Lord said, "From this day forward, O lady of bowed limbs, I am your slave, purchased by your ascetic penances," she immediately cast off the exhaustion born of her vows; for hardship, when rewarded with its fruit, restores one to newness of life.
Then Gaurī privately instructed her friend, who was the soul of all things:
"Let the Lord of Mountains be made the authority for my giving."
Having been addressed with that message by her, she shone silently toward her beloved,
like a mango branch with the face of a cuckoo at its tip in the springtime when it has been approached.
Having promised "So be it" and with great difficulty dismissing Umā,
the destroyer of Smara called to mind the seven seers who consist of light.
Illuminating the sky with their circles of light, those ascetics,
together with Arundhatī, suddenly appeared before the Lord.
They bathed in the currents of the celestial Gaṅgā, where waves scattered the blossoms of the Mandāra trees upon the banks,
and which were scented with the ichor of the elephants of the quarters.
Wearing pearl sacred threads and golden bark garments,
with jeweled rosaries in their hands, they had taken up the life of mendicants like wish-fulfilling trees.
They were constantly gazed upon with reverence by the thousand-rayed sun, whose horses moved downward and whose banner was bent low.
With the earth lifted up by his clinging, vine-like arms,
they found rest upon the tusk of the Great Boar during the calamity of universal dissolution.
Because they brought forth the remainder of the creation immediately after the Source of the Universe,
those ancient ones are celebrated by the knowers of antiquity as "the Creators" (dhātṛ).
Even as ascetics, they were enjoying the fruits of their former pure austerities that had reached full maturity.
Standing in their midst, that virtuous woman, her eyes fixed upon her husband’s feet,
shone intensely like the personified perfection of asceticism— Arundhatī herself.
The Lord beheld those sages without distinction of respect or lack thereof;
for whether one is woman or man, this indifference is not misplaced, since virtuous conduct is what is honored by the wise.
Upon seeing her, Śambhu felt a great longing for a wife;
indeed, virtuous wives are the fundamental means for performing religious rites.
When Śarva had even by means of dharma caused his own station to be established toward Pārvatī,
the mind of Kāma, fearing his former offense, was restored to breath.
Then all those sages, learned in the Vedas, having honored the Teacher of the World,
spoke these words with their skin bristling with joy.
That Brahman which has been correctly recited, that which has been offered into the fire according to the rule,
and that austerity which has been practiced— the fruit of all that has today ripened for us.
O Sovereign of the worlds, you have placed us within the range of your own mind— a realm that lies beyond the reach of even our desires.
Whoever dwells in your mind is already the best among the accomplished; how much more so he who dwells in the mind of you, the source of Brahmā!
We have indeed ascended to a station higher than both the sun and the moon;
today, however, it is even higher still, through the grace of your remembrance.
We hold ourselves in high esteem because of your regard for us;
generally, it is the highest honor that inspires confidence in one's own virtues.
O Virūpākṣa, why should that joy of ours which arises from meditating upon you be announced to you? For you are the inner self of all embodied beings.
You have been seen directly, yet we do not truly know you;
be gracious and tell us of yourself, for you do not abide within the path of the intellects.
Is it that by which you create the manifest, or that by which you sustain it?
Or are you the destroyer of the universe? Which of these is this portion of yours?
Alternatively, O Lord, let this very great request stand aside for now;
first command us regarding those things that appear as soon as they are thought of—what shall we do?
Then the Supreme Lord, augmenting the slender radiance of the moon resting upon his crest with the bright rays of his teeth, replied:
It is known to you that none of my activities are for my own sake;
indeed, I am indicated as being of such a nature by these eight forms.
Thus, like a cloud besought by cātaka birds parched with thirst,
I was entreated for offspring by the gods who had been oppressed by their enemies.
Therefore, I desire to bring Pārvatī for the birth of my own son,
just as a sacrificer brings the fire-drill wood for the production of the consumer of the oblation.
For our sake, you must request Himālaya for her;
for relationships properly established do not admit of alteration.
Know that I too have not been deceived, for I am joined in relationship with him who is exalted, steadfast, and who bears the burden of the earth. (Ks 6.30)
"You should not be instructed thus regarding the matter of the maiden;
for the virtuous follow the conduct established by you. (Ks 6.31)
Even the noble Arundhatī ought to exert herself in this matter;
for generally, in such affairs, housewives possess great confidence.
Therefore, let us set out for Oṣadhiprastha, the city of Himavat, for the sake of success;
there, at this great waterfall of the Mahākośī, we shall meet once again.
When that foremost of self-restrained men was about to be married,
the ascetics devoted to Prajāpati abandoned their shame regarding worldly possessions.
Then, having said "Excellent," the circle of sages departed;
the Blessed One also reached the first designated location.
And those supreme sages, having flown through the sky which was as dark as a sword-blade,
reached Oṣadhiprastha with a speed equal to that of thought.
Having surpassed Alakā as it were, the abode of the wealth of the Vasus,
it was established as if by vomiting forth the overflow of heaven.
Encircled by the flow of the Gaṅgā, with medicinal herbs blazing within its ramparts,
and possessing great jeweled stone pillars, it was enchanting even in its state of seclusion.
There, the elephants had conquered their fear of lions, the horses were born from the wombs of serpents,
the yakṣas and kimpuruṣas were the citizens, and the women were forest deities.
There, the sounds of drums produced by the hands are distinguished from the echoes of clouds clinging to the mountain peaks, which are otherwise indistinguishable from them.
There, by the very wish-fulfilling trees with their swaying branch-cloths,
the splendor of house-hanging banners was produced without the effort of the citizens.
Where, in crystal palaces at night in the banquet halls,
the reflections of the stars serve as offerings.
There, by the light of medicinal herbs,
women going to meet their lovers at night could find their way even when they were unaccustomed to darkness on cloudy days.
In that [state], youth is the limit of life; the affliction is the flower-armed god (Kāma);
and sleep, arising from the exhaustion of passion, is the reversal of consciousness.
There, by means of their anger— manifested through knitted brows, trembling lips, and the pointing of graceful fingers— the beloveds were made to seek the women's favor.
And his outer grove was the fragrant Gandhamādana, where travelers among the Vidyādharas slept in the shade of the Saṃtānaka trees.
Then those divine sages, beholding the city of Himavat,
considered that well-earned merit aimed at attaining heaven to be nothing but a deception.
At the mountain’s summit, they descended with speed, watched by the gatekeepers with upturned faces,
while their masses of matted hair remained as motionless as painted fires.
Descending from the sky,
that succession of sages shone like a row of suns within the waters, with the elders at their head.
Taking the guest-offering for those worthy of honor, the Mountain went out from afar to meet them,
causing the earth to bow down by his footsteps, which were heavy with the weight of his essence.
With lips copper-colored like the mineral ore, tall in stature, and with arms as massive as deodar trees,
he was by his very nature broad-chested like a rock, clearly manifest as the Himalaya.
Accompanied by honors performed according to the prescribed rites, and personally showing the way,
he was led by those of pure deeds into the inner apartments.
There, having taken his seat upon one made of cane,
the Mountain, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to the lords who were seated there.
Your appearance has occurred to us unexpectedly, like rain without the rising of clouds, or fruit without visible flowers; it seems to me as if it has arrived without being anticipated.
Through your grace, I consider myself— though formerly deluded as if awakened, like iron turned to gold, and as if ascended from earth to heaven.
"From this day forward, I am to be approached by all beings for the sake of purification;
for that which has been occupied by Arhats is declared to be a sacred ford (tīrtha)."
O best of the twice-born, I consider myself purified by two things alone:
by the descent of the Gaṅgā upon my head and by the water from your feet which has washed them.
I consider my own body, though it possesses two forms— the mobile in the state of being your servant and the immobile marked by your footprints— to have been bestowed with grace upon both.
My limbs, though they pervade the ends of the quarters, are not sufficient for the swelling joy that arises from your high regard for me.
Not only has the darkness situated within the cave been dispelled for you by the sight of the luminous ones,
but even the darkness beyond the realm of passion (rajas) has been cast out from my interior.
"I see nothing that ought to be done by you; if there were anything, why would it not be possible?
I suspect your departure here is solely for the sake of purifying me."
Nevertheless, you ought to grant me a command for a while;
for servants exist to receive the grace of being employed by their masters.
"Here we are, and here are my wives; this maiden is the very life of our lineage.
Tell me what you require of these, for there is no attachment to external things."
Having spoken thus, Himālaya proclaimed that very same matter again, as it were, through an echo spreading from the mouth of the cave.
Then the sages urged Aṅgiras, the leader among those cited as examples in various matters; he, in turn, replied to the Mountain.
All this is fitting for you, and even beyond it;
your loftiness is equal to that of the peaks of the mind.
It is fitting that they call you Viṣṇu, whose nature is stable; for indeed, you have become the womb and the support for all beings, both moving and unmoving.
How could the serpent have supported the earth with hoods as soft as lotus stalks,
had you not held it up from the very base of the netherworld?
With their stainless lineages unbroken and unrestrained like the waves of the ocean,
both your fame and your rivers purify the worlds through their merit.
Just as the Gaṅgā is praised for being touched by the foot of the Supreme Lord, so too is she praised because of you, her second source, who are like a towering mountain peak.
The greatness of Hari pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards;
and that same greatness, which was manifested when he strode the three worlds as Trivikrama, is innate to you.
By you, who have taken your place among those who partake in the sacrificial offerings,
the lofty golden peak of Sumeru has been rendered futile.
You have bestowed all your hardness upon the stationary body;
this form of yours, however, is bowed with devotion for the sake of propitiating the virtuous.
Listen then to the purpose of our coming; that task is yours alone, while we here share only a portion of it by virtue of providing instruction on what is beneficial.
He who bears aloft the word "Īśvara," accompanied by the half-moon, which is endowed with qualities such as *aṇimā* and untouched by any other person.
By means of the earth and the other elements, which possess mutually imagined capacities,
this entire universe is supported within the Self, just as a carriage is borne by draft animals on a road.
That which yogins discern as residing within the field (kṣetra), and which the wise call the state beyond the fear of returning— Ks_6.77.
Śambhu, the bestower of boons and the direct witness of all deeds, has himself chosen your daughter, using words transmitted through us.
You ought to unite that purpose with the daughter of Bhārata as if she were his own wealth;
for a daughter bestowed upon a virtuous husband is not to be grieved for by her father.
As long as these beings, both stationary and moving,
regard her as their mother, so too is the Lord the father of the world.
Immediately after bowing to the blue-throated Lord Śiva,
the gods brighten her feet with the rays of their crest-jewels.
Umā is the bride, you are the giver, and we here are the petitioners;
Śambhu is the groom—indeed, this is the ordinance sufficient for the exaltation of your lineage.
Become the father of the Universal Teacher through the rite of marriage with his daughter— he who is himself unstudied yet praised, and who is worthy of worship yet has no other to worship him.
While the celestial sage was speaking thus, Pārvatī, standing by her father’s side with her face cast downward,
began counting the petals of her play-lotus.
Although his desire was fulfilled, Śaila gazed at the face of Menā;
for householders, in matters concerning their daughters, are generally guided by the eyes of their wives.
Menā also approved all that her husband desired to do;
for devoted wives never fail in what is pleasing to their husbands.
Having reflected with the thought, "This is the most appropriate answer here," he took his daughter, adorned with auspicious ornaments, at the conclusion of his words.
"Come, my child; you have been designated as alms for the Universal Soul.
The sages are seekers, and I have attained the fruit of being a householder."
Having said this much to his daughter, the Mountain spoke to the sages:
"This wife of the Three-eyed One bows before you all."
Having rejoiced in the mountain’s speech, which was noble in its fulfillment of their desired purpose,
