they strengthened Ambikā with blessings that were already ripe for fruition.
Arundhatī placed upon her lap that bashful woman, whose golden ear-ornament had slipped down due to the intensity of her prostration.
And he dispelled the grief of his mother, whose face was bathed in tears and who was overwhelmed by affection for her daughter,
by means of the virtues of that bridegroom who had never belonged to another before.
Questioned at that moment by the kinsman of Hara regarding the auspicious date for the wedding,
they— clad in bark garments— announced it to be three days hence and departed.
Having taken leave of the Himalaya and looked once more upon the wielder of the trident (Śūlin),
and having reported the matter accomplished to him, they departed for the sky, dismissed by him.
Even Paśupati passed those days with great difficulty, longing for union with the Daughter of the Mountain;
for what other person, however powerless, would these emotions not disturb, since they affect even that Lord?
Then, on a lunar day marked by the waxing of the moon— the lord of medicinal herbs— and endowed with the quality of being the friend of the zodiac sign,
Himavat, his kinsmen assembled, performed the ritual initiation for the marriage of his daughter.
With the preparations for wedding festivities underway in every house, the womenfolk were busily occupied;
through their mutual affection, the city and the inner apartments of the mountain seemed like a single household.
With its great highways strewn with *saṃtānaka* flowers and its rows of banners fashioned from Chinese silks,
it shone like another heaven, ablaze with the luster of golden archways.
Though she was but one among a row of sons, Umā became a special source of relief for her parents— as if seen after a long time, as if risen from the dead, and as if her marriage were now at hand.
Having received blessings, she passed from one lap to another and enjoyed one ornament after another;
though divided among various relatives, her affection for the mountain clan found its sole abode in her.
At the auspicious moment when the moon was in conjunction with the Uttaraphalgunī asterism,
the female relatives who had husbands and sons performed the funeral rites upon her body.

She adorned herself with the ointments and finery for the bath, which possessed a luster interrupted by sprouts of *dūrvā* grass resembling white mustard seeds, and which was like a silken garment without a navel, bearing the mark of a reed.
And that young woman shone as she came into contact with the arrow of the rite of initiation,
like the crescent of the moon being kindled by the hand of the sun at the end of the dark fortnight.

The women led her toward the dais; she had had the oil from her body removed with a paste of *lodhra*, her limbs were anointed with fragrant unguents made of dried *kāleyaka*, and she wore a garment suitable for the consecration.
Upon this surface of laid-out vaidūrya stones, variegated with patterns of unperforated pearls,
they bathed her to the accompaniment of musical instruments, using water from jars of the eight auspicious substances.
With her limbs purified by an auspicious bath and wearing garments fit for her husband’s departure,
she shone like the earth when it has received the sprinkling of rain from a finished storm and its kāśa flowers are in full bloom.
From that place, they led her— who was covered with a canopy and attended by four jeweled pillars—
to the center of the wedding altar, where seats had been prepared, and she was escorted there by women devoted to their husbands.
Having seated that slender woman there facing the east, the women sat before her for a moment;
though the means of adornment were at hand, their eyes were drawn away by the natural beauty of her form.
A certain woman bound up her hair— its moisture having been dispelled by the heat of incense and containing flowers within—
with a pale madhūka wreath entwined with dūrvā grass in a magnificent braid.
They applied white aloe-wood paste to her body and fashioned decorative patterns with yellow orpiment;
she stood surpassing the beauty of the triple-streamed Ganges, whose sandy banks are marked by *cakravāka* birds.
Surpassing the lotus with its settled bees and the orb of the moon accompanied by a streak of clouds,
the beauty of her face— with its well-known tresses— cut short any further discussion of resemblance.
On her cheek— which was dry from the lodhra-ash paste applied to her ear and rendered intensely pale by the application of yellow orpiment—
the sprout of a barley grain, having attained a state of supreme excellence, captivated the eyes of all beholders.
And the lower lip of her whose limbs were well-proportioned— divided by a line, its color slightly polished with beeswax,
and bearing the fruit of approaching loveliness— attained an indescribable splendor through its quivering movements.
"Touch the crescent moon upon your husband's head with this," her friend said jokingly;
having had her feet anointed and received a blessing, she struck her back wordlessly with a garland.
Having observed her eyes, which were as lovely as the petals of a well-grown lotus,
the adorners did not apply black collyrium to them out of a perception of any particular beauty in her eyes, but rather because it was auspicious.
Like a creeper with blossoming flowers, like the night with rising stars,
or like a river with birds alighting upon it, she shone as her ornaments were being fastened.
Beholding herself shining in the reflection of the mirror, the large-eyed woman became eager for Hara’s arrival; for the purpose of women’s dress is indeed the sight of their beloved.
Then his mother, lifting up his face— upon which were attached pure ivory ear-ornaments— took auspicious moist yellow orpiment and realgar with her two fingers.
Mena somehow managed to turn that very first desire, which had grown ever stronger since the budding of Umā’s breasts,
into the marriage-consecration tilaka for her daughter.
And with eyes clouded by tears, she tied on her wrist that woolen amulet-string, which had been fashioned into a particular shape and was being smoothed out by the fingers of her nurse.
Clad in fresh silk garments, she shone even more brightly as she held up the mirror, like the shore of the milk-ocean with its mass of foam, or like an autumn night with a full moon.
Having caused that family pillar to be prostrated before the honored ancestral deities, the mother—
skilled in what ought to be done— had the virtuous women perform the ritual clasping of her feet in due order.
"May you obtain undivided love from your husband"—thus was Umā addressed by them as she bowed;
yet by her, who shared half his body, even the blessings of affectionate kinsmen were surpassed.
Having performed every duty for her in accordance with her desires and her power,
the skillful mountain king remained in the assembly hall where his friend was present, awaiting the arrival of the bull-bannered god.
Meanwhile, on Mount Kubera, the bridegroom’s ornaments— befitting his previous marriage—
were respectfully arranged before the Lord of the City by his devoted mothers.
Out of respect for him, that Goddess, whose splendor was her auspicious ornaments, was touched by the Lord only with his own hand;
for she attained a different state within the beloved form of the All-pervading One, who was himself the bridegroom.
The ashes themselves became his white cosmetic paste; the skull alone was the splendor of his stainless crest-ornament;
and the elephant hide itself, marked with yellow pigment at its edges, took on the nature of fine silk garments.
That eye which shines from within the conch-shell, with its pure brown pupil set deep inside,
became the very act of applying a forehead mark made of yellow orpiment when she was in his presence.

Just as the lordly serpents, who were about to be made into ornaments, remained in their respective places, so too did the splendor of the jewels upon their hoods remain, while only their bodies underwent transformation.
What need is there for Śiva to seize the crest-jewel from whose crown it is constantly eclipsed by the moon— even during the day— with its rays emitted and its spot unmanifest due to its infancy?
Thus, the creator of the celebrated rules of costume, whose sole source of power was his own majesty,
beheld himself reflected in the sword brought forward by the attendant attendants.

Supporting himself on the arm of Nandin, he set out for Gopatī, having ascended that mountain whose broad back was covered with a tiger skin and which, due to his devotion, appeared diminished in its vast proportions like Mount Kailāsa.
The Mothers, following after the god, their ear-ornaments swaying from the jolting of their own vehicles,
made the sky appear like a bed of lotuses with their faces, pale as the pollen of a halo of light.
And behind those women of golden luster, Kālī, adorned with skull ornaments,
shone forth like a row of dark clouds accompanied by cranes, with a hundred lightning flashes cast far ahead.
Then, the sound of auspicious musical instruments, raised by the hosts of attendants leading the Trident-bearer,
resonated as it penetrated the peaks of the celestial chariots, announcing the time for service to the gods.
The Thousand-rayed One (the Sun) took up for him a new parasol fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ;
with his crown not far from that silk garment, he shone like the Ganges falling upon his head.
Then the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, having taken embodied form, waited upon the god with chowries,
appearing like two rivers flowing toward the ocean even though their forms had been transformed, accompanied by swans.
The first Creator and the Person himself, marked with the Śrīvatsa, followed him,
increasing his majesty with the cry "Victory!", as one increases a fire with an oblation.
That single form divided itself threefold; their commonality is the relationship of superior and inferior.
Sometimes Viṣṇu is the elder to Hara, sometimes Hari is the elder to him, and sometimes Brahmā is the elder to those two; yet even those two are the first-born of the Creator.

The world-protectors, headed by Puruhūta, their attire subdued by the manifestation of auspicious marks, signaled Nandin to grant them an audience; directed by him, they bowed with palms joined in reverence.
With a movement of his head he honored Brahmā, with his speech Hari, and with a smile the slayer of Vṛtra;
with a mere glance he honored all the gods without exception, according to their respective rank.
He first offered him a blessing of victory; then, with a smile, he said to the Seven Sages:
"Since this marriage sacrifice has been commenced, you have all been chosen by me as the *adhvaryu* priests."
While his heroic deeds against Tripura were being sung by masters of music led by Viśvāvasu,
he who bears the crescent moon as his crest crossed the path that cannot be traversed by those whose vision is impaired by darkness.
A horse, moving with a playful gait and adorned with jingling golden bells, carried him;
it repeatedly shook its long, thick-set ears as if its hooves were stuck in mud from striking the riverbank.
In a mere moment, he reached the city protected by the Lord of Mountains, which had not yet been subjected to an attack by an enemy;
he was being drawn forward, as it were, by the glances of Śiva fixed upon the city ahead, like golden threads.
Near its edge, the Lord, whose throat was dark as a rain-cloud, being watched by the citizens with upturned faces out of curiosity,
descended from the path marked by his own arrow and reached the surface of the nearby ground.

The sovereign of mountains, pleased by his arrival, went out to meet him with throngs of elephants mounted by kinsmen endowed with supernatural powers, as if with his own ridges where trees were in full bloom.
At the city gate, whose cover had been lifted, the two hosts of gods and mountain-dwellers met,
their clamor spreading afar, like two floods of water from separate banks that have broken through a single dam.
The mountain became modest when he was saluted by Hara, who is worshipped by the three worlds;
for previously, his head had been so far bowed down by [Hara’s] majesty that he did not even perceive it.

With the beauty of his face blooming from the touch of joy, he took the lead before his son-in-law and led him into the magnificent palace, where flowers were strewn as far as the ankles along the market paths.
At that moment, in the palace rows of the city’s beauties who were longing for a sight of the Lord, there occurred such activities as they abandoned all other tasks.
As one woman rushed suddenly toward the path of light, she did not even notice her braid of hair, from which flowers were falling as they unwound; though held by her hand, it was not secured at all.
A certain woman, having cast aside her forefoot— which had been held by her hairdresser and was still dripping with dye—
hurriedly departed from the window, leaving a trail marked by red lac as she abandoned her graceful gait.
Having adorned her right eye with collyrium, another woman, whose left eye was thus deprived of its beauty,
approached the window in that very manner, still carrying the applicator stick.
Another woman, her gaze directed through the lattice window, did not fasten her girdle which had slipped during her departure;
she stood holding up her garment with a hand whose brilliance was enhanced by the ornament resting upon her navel.
At that moment, as she rose in haste with her body only half-adorned, her girdle— slipping at every ill-placed step—
remained as nothing more than a thread fastened to the base of her big toe.

With their faces, filled with the scent of wine, filling the interiors of the windows, those women of intense curiosity made the casements appear as if adorned with thousand-petaled lotuses, their flickering eyes being the black bees.
Meanwhile, the moon-crested Lord reached the royal highway, which was crowded with banners and adorned with lofty arches,
making even the palace turrets appear doubly radiant as if bathed in moonlight during the day.
Drinking him in with their eyes as his sole object of sight, the women did not turn toward other sensory objects;
for the activity of their remaining senses had entered, as it were, entirely through their eyes alone.
It is fitting that this difficult penance was performed for his sake even by the delicate Aparṇā;
for what woman would not consider her purpose fulfilled by merely obtaining his servitude, let alone by lying upon his lap?
If the Creator had not joined this pair, whose mutual splendor is so desirable,
the effort expended in fashioning their beauty would have been in vain for the Lord of Creatures.
Surely his body was not consumed by the god of the flower-arrowed weapon out of rising wrath;
rather, I think that upon beholding this deity, Kāma himself abandoned his own form out of shame.

Having thus entered into this alliance, by good fortune the King of Mountains will, through the power of the Lord, address his head— which is already high from supporting the earth— with even greater height, as it was long desired by his heart's wish.

Thus, listening to the ear-pleasing stories of the women sporting on the Oṣadhiprastha mountain, the Three-eyed Lord reached the abode of Himālaya, where handfuls of parched grain were being crushed by their armlets.

Having descended there, with a hand extended by Acyuta, he entered the inner courtyards of the Lord of Mountains— which had previously been traversed by the Lotus-Seated One— just as the sun enters from an autumn cloud.

Following him came the gods headed by Indra, the supreme ṛṣis led by the Seven Sages, and the hosts of mountain-dwellers; they approached him as those seeking the highest goal approach a praiseworthy undertaking.
There, the Lord duly accepted the seat, the water for honoring with jewels, the honeyed milk product from a cow,
and the two new silk garments brought by the Mountain King— all except for the recitation of mantras.
Clad in fine linen, he was led by humble guards of the inner apartments to the presence of his bride,
just as the ocean, with its rows of foam clearly visible, is led toward the shore by the rays of the new moon.

By that maiden, whose moon-like facial radiance was fully developed, Śiva became one whose lotus-eyes blossomed and whose waters of mind were serene, just as the world becomes when joined with autumn.
In their meditative absorptions, the eyes of the two, timid and somewhat fixed yet withdrawn, experienced for a moment the restraint of shame, though they remained longing for one another.

The Eight-formed Lord took her hand, which was brought forward with the weight of the mountain and possessed copper-colored fingers; it was as if he were grasping the first sprout of the God of Love, whose body was hidden within Umā’s form, before that god could fearfully grow.
A thrill of horripilation appeared on Umā, and the bull-bannered god’s fingers became moist with sweat;
through the joining of their hands, the activity of the God of Love seemed as if divided equally between the two.

When another bride and groom, having performed the ritual grasping of hands, attain supreme splendor through the conjunction of the presence of these two [the sun and moon], what can be said of the glory belonging to both of them?
From the circumambulation of the blazing fire,
that pair shone forth like day and night joined together at the slopes of Mount Meru.
Having led the couple three times around the fire, the family priest caused the bride— who had closed her eyes at the touch of the tips of his fingers—
to perform the scattering of parched grain into those kindled flames.
Following the instruction of her elders, she brought the fragrant handful of parched grain-smoke to her mouth;
its crest, gliding over her cheek, for a moment attained the state of an ear-lotus.

Due to the taking up of the customary smoke, the bride’s face became such that the lines of her cheeks were slightly moist and reddened, the dark collyrium on her eyes was beginning to fade, and the barley-ear ornaments were withered.
The twice-born said to the bride: "O child, this fire is your witness from the outset regarding the marriage;
you must practice the dharma together with your husband Śiva, free from all hesitation."
Having extended her ear until the end of the recitation, Bhavānī drank in those words of the Guru,
just as the earth first drinks the rain from Indra when parched by the intense heat of the summer season.
Being urged by her steadfast husband, who was eager to see her, to look at him, she raised her face and, with a throat choked by bashfulness, spoke with great difficulty: "He has been seen."
Thus, having performed the rites of marriage according to the prescribed rules by their priest,
the two of them bowed down to their parents— the progenitors of all beings— and to the Grandfather (Brahmā) seated upon his lotus throne.
"The bride was greeted by the Creator with the blessing, 'O auspicious one, may you give birth to heroes.
Though he was the Lord of Speech himself, he remained motionless with anxiety, despite being the eight-formed god."
Having approached the square altar prepared with the prescribed offerings, the husband and wife, seated upon golden thrones, performed the worldly rite of scattering moist grains of unhusked rice.
Above the two of them, Lakṣmī held a lotus-umbrella with a long stalk, its beauty enhanced by clusters of water droplets clinging to the edges of its petals, resembling a net of pearls.

And Sarasvatī, through her twofold application of speech— purified by grammatical refinement for the bridegroom, the most excellent of men, and composed with easily grasped constructions for the bride— extolled that couple.

For a moment, they watched the first performance of the Apsarases, in which the distinctions of the emotional states were manifested through the transitions, the passion was fixed upon various sentiments, and the graceful movements of the limbs were displayed.
At the conclusion of that [period], the gods, having prostrated before Hara— who had taken a wife— with their hands joined in reverence upon their crowns,
entreated him for the service of the five-arrowed god, whose form had been restored at the end of his curse.
The Blessed One, free from resentment, consented even to the employment of arrows against himself;
for indeed, a request made at the proper time by those who know how to act achieves success with their masters.
Then the moon-crested Lord, having dismissed those hosts of gods, took the daughter of the mountain king by the hand and entered the bridal chamber,
which was prepared with a bed upon the ground and graced by the beauty of the decorative lines on golden jars.
There, the Lord Śiva caused Gaurī— who was adorned with the bashfulness of her new marriage and who was averting her face when he made a gesture of lifting it—
to laugh secretly, even though she had managed to speak only with difficulty to her bed-friends by means of facial contortions produced by the Pramathas.

Immediately after the rite of joining hands, the body of the daughter of the Mountain King became enchanting due to the longing of love, as she was overcome by both emotion and trepidation toward Hara.
Though addressed, she did not offer a reply; though her garment was pulled away, she desired to depart;
and though she turned her back toward him, she nevertheless attended the bed for the sake of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
As Pārvatī lay there in feigned sleep out of curiosity, she cast her gaze toward her lover’s face;
when he opened his eyes with a smile, she closed her own as if struck by lightning.
Śaṅkara’s hand, placed upon her navel, was held back by her trembling [hand],
and thus her silk garment itself became loose, its knot having slipped far away.

Thus, when her beloved stood before her, she— distraught and having forgotten the instruction given by her friends that "Śaṅkara should be served in secret once your timidity has been subdued"— could not remember it.

Even though it concerned a non-existent thing, Pārvatī, perceiving with her glance the God of Love who was intent on asking a question for the sake of initiating a conversation, gave him an answer in the form of a nod of her head.

Having blocked his eyes with both palms, she, her garment snatched away, looked at the eye on the forehead of the wielder of the trident; distressed by her futile effort, she was left in a state of secret shame.
In kisses, [the husband] refrained from giving his lower lip; in embraces, he was merciless with his hands;
though the lover’s passion was thus tormented, the beloved wife found no way to retaliate against her lord.
Pārvatī endured that which her beloved gave— a kiss upon her uninjured lower lip and a fingernail-mark without a wound— as well as his tender lovemaking, but nothing else.
At the time of dawn, she did not allow her circle of friends— who were eager to question her about the events of the night—
to be free from curiosity out of modesty, yet she was inwardly in haste to tell them.
And beholding her lover seated behind her as she looked at herself in a mirror,
what various actions did she not perform out of shame, seeing her own reflection following his?
Seeing her youth enjoyed by the blue-throated god, the mother was comforted;
for, through being beloved by their husband, women of noble lineage dispel their mental grief for their mothers.
After some days, Śiva somehow engaged in dalliance with her;
as she gradually came to know the essence of amorous passion, she slowly abandoned her habitual aversion to the pains of sexual union.
Pressed against his chest, she embraced her beloved; she did not offer him the face he requested, and she loosely restrained his hand that had moved toward the playful gesture of grasping her girdle.

In just a few days, the love between those two became firmly rooted, resting upon one another— a love revealed by their gestures, free from any unpleasantness, full of endearments, and yet anxious at the thought of even momentary separation.
The bride was as enamored with that groom who resembled her own self as he was with her;
for the Ganges never departs from the ocean, and he too finds his sole satisfaction in the flavor of her mouth.
Having approached Śaṅkara, who was instructing her in the art of lovemaking, in secret,
that young woman acquired a proficiency which she then offered as her teacher’s fee.
With her sprout-like hand trembling from the pain, Ambikā momentarily cooled the bitten lower lip with the cool crescent moon upon the head of the Wielder of the Trident.
Even Śaṅkara gave his forehead eye— polluted by the powder from her hair during their kisses—
to the breath from Pārvatī’s mouth, which possessed the fragrance of a blooming lotus.
Thus, having favored his passion by indulging in the path of sensual pleasure,
the bull-bannered god dwelt for a full month with Umā in the abode of the king of mountains.
Having thus consoled the Himavat, who was afflicted by the sorrow of separation from his daughter,
the Self-born One wandered here and there, traveling with his bull of immeasurable gait.
Having reached Mount Meru, the skillful Marudāśugokṣaka enjoyed, with Pārvatī at his side,
beds made of golden shoots that were capable of enduring the pressure of amorous play.
While fresh droplets of nectar fell upon stones marked with the footprints of Padmanābha,
he dwelt on the slopes of Mount Mandara as a bee at the lotus-face of Pārvatī.
With her arms tightly bound around his neck, she who was terrified by the trumpeting of the elephant,
the Teacher of the World entered the bright moonlight upon Mount Ekapiṅgala.

Once, while he was sporting on the slopes of Mount Malaya, the southern breeze— shaking the sandalwood creepers and carrying the fragrance of cloves and saffron— dispelled his beloved’s fatigue like a flattering lover.
Struck by her beloved with a red lotus, her eyes closed at his touch,
Umā plunged into the river in the sky, her girdle doubled by the rows of fish.
Adorning her with pārijāta flowers worthy of the locks of Puloman’s daughter,
the Three-eyed Lord was gazed upon with longing for a long time by the celestial nymphs in the Nandana grove.
Having thus experienced celestial and earthly pleasures in the company of his beloved, Śaṅkara once entered Mount Gandhamādana when the sun was turning red in the heat of the afternoon.
There, resting upon a surface of golden stone and beholding the sun within the range of his vision,
he addressed his partner in dharma, who was leaning against his left arm.
Having transferred the lotus-like luster from the two parts of his face reddened by twilight to your two eyes, as it were,
this lord of day now withdraws his light at the end of the world, like the Lord of Creatures withdrawing the universe.
As the sun sinks low, casting its rays far away from the spray of water droplets,
these mountain torrents of your father’s domain lose their rainbow-like enclosures.
Of the two cakravāka birds in the lake, who were biting the filaments of their lotuses, crying out with throats convulsed,
and clinging to one another, the small distance between them became no small thing.
Leaving their usual daily spot, the elephants take up water scented with the broken branches of *sallakī* trees— water filled with bees clinging to lotuses— in order to depart at dawn.
Behold, O you of measured speech, how the sun, hanging at the edge of the western quarter,
has fashioned with its long reflection upon the waters of the lake a causeway as if made of gold.
Having waded across the pond after the intense heat has passed,
the leaders of the forest boar herds emerge, scattering about like fanged serpents that have snapped off the curved sprouts of lotus roots.
Perched upon the crest of this tree, its circle of plumage as bright as the essence of gold,
this peacock seems to drink up the waning day whose heat has passed, O lady with full-thighed limbs.
On one side, the sky appears like a lake that has become clearly muddy due to the onset of the darkness of the eastern quarter,
its water of heat having been drawn away by the sun, leaving only a small remnant.
With deer entering the courtyards of the huts and young trees lush from the watering of their roots,
the hermitages— where the sacrificial cows have entered and the fires have been kindled— bear a manifest splendor.
Even when its bud is closed, the lotus remains for a moment with its opening slightly ajar,
as if out of affection it were granting an interval for the bee to take up residence within.
The western quarter shines with its foremost rays of immeasurable extent,
adorned by the ruddy sun like a young maiden graced with a tilaka-mark of bandhujīva flowers upon her hair.
Accompanied by thousands of chants, those who subsist on the warmth of the sun's rays praise the sun— whose splendor is scattered like fire— with voices as enchanting as the heart of a chariot-horse.
Thus, with horses whose necks are bent low, whose eyes are struck by the chowries on their ears,
and whose manes are curved like a yoke, he sets toward the great ocean at the end of the day.
When the sun has set, the sky remains as if fast asleep; such is the course of great splendor:
it illuminates only so long as it has risen, for once it has fallen, it leads indeed to closing.
The body of the sun, followed by the twilight, is worthy of worship as it is offered upon the peak of the setting mountain;
how could he, who was previously honored at its rising, not follow him in times of distress?
O lady with curly hair, these millions of clouds, crimson, yellow, and brownish-red,
appear as if they have been beautifully decorated with wicks by this twilight, as if to say, "You shall see them."
Behold the evening sunlight, as it were, distributed by the sun among the manes of lions, the leaf-bearing trees of the mountains, and the peaks of the minerals.
O Daughter of the Mountain King, these ascetics, who know the ritual injunctions, perform their reverential salutations with handfuls of purifying water;
attentive to purification, they recite the hidden Veda at the time of twilight.
Therefore, you ought to grant me this brief moment for the observance I have undertaken;
O sweet-spoken one, your circle of friends, skilled in diversion, will amuse you.
Then, parting her lips while intent on disregarding her husband’s words,
the daughter of the Mountain King spoke pointlessly to Vijayā, who stood nearby.
The Lord also performed the ritual appropriate for the end of the day according to the prescribed mantras;
then, approaching Pārvatī—who remained silent out of resentment—he spoke to her again with a smile.
Abandon your anger, O you who are prone to groundless wrath; I have been saluted by the twilight, not by any other woman.
Do you not recognize your partner in dharma, whose conduct is equal to that of a ruddy sheldrake?
O fair-limbed one, that very body which was formerly cast off by the Self-born One among the created ancestors—
since it now partakes in both setting and rising, O proud lady, I hold it in high esteem.
O daughter of the mountain king, look now at her who stands here, afflicted by the increase of darkness—
on one side lined with tamāla trees on the bank, like a river flowing with mineral pigments.
The western quarter bears the twilight glow of the sun that has just set— a streak of red—
like a blood-stained dagger cast askance upon the battlefield of war.
O long-eyed one, when the light produced at the junction of night and day is obstructed by Mount Sumeru,
this unrestrained, blinding darkness spreads throughout the quarters.
The movement of his vision is neither upward nor downward, neither to the side nor in front nor behind;
this world, enveloped by a mass of darkness, proceeds like dwelling in a womb during the night.

Whether pure or turbid, stable or moving, crooked or endowed with the quality of rectitude—all of this is made uniform by darkness; fie on the greatness of the wicked, whose inner essence has been stolen away!
Surely the Lord of Sacrificers rises to dispel the darkness of night;
O lotus-faced one, the face of the eastern quarter is covered with pollen as if with ketaka flowers.
The night, its form veiled by the Mandara mountain, is perceived through the moon along with the stars;
you, having met with your dear friend, shall likewise hear my words from behind, as if they were being spoken to you.
With its exit blocked until the end of the day, this lunar orb emits the very same bodily luster and smiles previously seen,
like a secret of the quarters revealed by the night.

Behold: the pair of cakravāka birds, separated by a great distance, imitates the sky and the lake whose waters are marked by the reflection of the moon, which possesses the luster of the fruit of the *pakvaphalinī* tree.

It would be possible for you to pluck with the hollow of your fingertips the hands of the Lord of Herbs, tender as the tips of unripened young grass, for the purpose of fashioning them into ear-ornaments at your new awakening.
As if grasping the mass of darkness with its rays like fingers,
the moon kisses the face of night, whose lotus-eyes are closed in bud.
Behold, Pārvatī, the vault of the sky, its darkness partially pierced by the rays of the new moon,
appears like the Mānasa lake brightening after being fouled by the body of an elephant.
Having abandoned its state of being red, this moon has arisen with a perfectly pure orb;
indeed, no transformation born of the defects of time occurs in those whose nature is stainless, for their rising is firm.
The moonlight rests upon the high places, while the night’s darkness is intent on taking refuge in the low;
surely the Creator has fashioned here the course of virtues and faults according to their own likeness.
With drops of water from moonstones set in motion by the rays of the moon, the mountain awakens these peacocks sleeping on the trees of its slopes at an unseasonable hour.

"O beautiful one, look! The moon, having become curious, seems now to be eager to count the strings of pearl necklaces as if they were shimmering upon the tops of the wish-fulfilling trees with its rays."
Due to its state of being both elevated and depressed, this moonlight on the mountain, mingled with shadows,
shines like the ichor-marked ash applied in various patterns upon a rutting elephant.
The night-lily, having released the humming of the bees, suddenly splits apart from its very roots, as if unable to bear the weight of the moonlight it has inhaled and now exhaled.
Behold, O passionate one: as the wind blows, the garment hanging from the wish-fulfilling tree—its true form obscured by the pure moonlight—is revealed only as it turns back upon itself.
It is possible to ruffle your tresses with these fingers— delicate as fallen flowers from the lower branches of trees,
their tips pale like the moonlight frayed by leaves.
O lovely-faced one, this moon is joined with the tremulous orb of the yoga-star,
like a bridegroom united with a bride at her first initiation who trembles with apprehension.
Upon your two cheeks— which are as fair as the shafts of a reed freshly cut, radiant with their shimmering reflections,
and bright as the moon’s orb set within your eyes— the moonlight seems to grow.
Carrying for herself the honey of the Kalpa-tree placed within a vessel of red ruby,
this presiding deity of the Gandhamādana forest has approached you as you stand here.
Your face is naturally fragrant with moist filaments and possesses eyes red with passion;
O playful woman, what further quality will intoxication add to it now that it has found its dwelling place here?
"Or rather, let your circle of friends, who possess devotion for the venerable one, partake of this which kindles the god of love"—
having spoken thus nobly, Śaṅkara made Ambikā drink the beverage.

Pārvatī, though subject to a transformation arising from that union which was enchanting even to the virtuous and fashioned by the inconceivable workings of destiny, became like a mango tree attaining the state of a *sahakāra* (a fragrant mango).

At that moment, as their modesty was cast aside and they desired no longer to remain on the bed, the fair-faced woman became subject to the will of both: the wielder of the trident and the god of passion.
With eyes rolling, speech faltering, covered in beads of perspiration, and wearing a causeless smile—
the Lord did not yet drink in Umā’s face with his eyes, but rather with his mouth for a long time.
Wearing that girdle of suspended gold which was difficult to bear due to the weight of her hips,
the Lord, whose splendor was accumulated through meditation, entered the private chamber of precious stone in solitude.

There, accompanied by his beloved, he reclined upon a couch with a white swan-patterned coverlet, as beautiful to behold as a sandbank on the Jāhnavī, like the Lord of Rohiṇī resting upon an autumnal cloud.
With her hair disheveled, her sandalwood paste rubbed away, her fingernails pressed into him in reverse, and full of passion,
Pārvatī’s love-making— marked by the snapping of her girdle-string— was not yet satiated.
Only when the rows of stars had bent low, out of compassion for his beloved,
did he— his chest embraced by her— engage in the curious sport of closing his eyes.
At dawn, that wise prince, who was worthy of praise, awoke to auspicious songs sung by *kinnaras* accompanied by melodies in the *kaishika* mode, as if with lakes of golden lotuses.
For a moment, the couple relaxed their embrace, their minds agitated by fear;
then the breezes from the edge of the Gandhamādana forest began to blow, heralding the blooming of lotuses.
At that moment, Hara, his eyes captivated by the rows of nail-marks at the base of her thighs,
stopped his beloved as she was adjusting her loosened garment.

Full of passion, he took delight in beholding his beloved’s face, its eyes clouded by sleeplessness, its lower lip deeply bitten by her teeth, its hair disheveled, and its forehead-mark (tilaka) smudged.

Therefore, at the end of the night, she did not abandon her bed— even though it was spotless— marked by the red dye from her feet, with its coverlet unevenly torn and its waistband knotted in the middle with loose threads.
Desiring to enjoy day and night the nectar of his beloved’s face, which generates an increase of joy,
he became invisible to those longing for his sight until the announcement of his victory.
For Śambhu, who was united with her there, three days and nights passed as if they were but a single night, exceeding even a hundred seasons;
yet he did not become satiated with the pleasures of love, like a fire within the ocean that never quenches its thirst for its waters.
